3       B.   The Instant Motion                                              
4       On April 4, 2023, Andrews propounded RFP No. 38, Set One, to Plaintiff.  (ECF 
5  Nos. 37-1 at 1–2 (“Folan Decl.”) ¶ 2; 37-1 at 4–10 (“Mot. Ex. A”).)  Plaintiff responded

21       The parties met and conferred regarding Plaintiff’s response and Andrews’ request 
22  for supplementation.  (Folan Decl. ¶ 3.)  After requesting and receiving two extensions, the 
23  parties raised the discovery dispute with the Court on August 31, 2023.  (See ECF Nos. 26; 
24  27; 28; 30; 34.)  The Court held an informal discovery conference on September 20, 2023 
25  (ECF No. 35), after which a briefing schedule was issued (ECF No. 36).  Andrews’ timely 
26  motion seeking to compel further response and production of documents to RFP No. 38 
27  followed.  (ECF No. 37.)

1  II.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                      
2       The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure authorize parties to obtain discovery of any 
3  nonprivileged  information  discoverable  under  Rule  26  if  it  is  (1)  relevant,  and  (2) 
4  proportional to the needs of the case.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1).  Rule 26(b)(1), as amended 
5  in 2015, provides that parties—                                           
6                                                                            
        may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to 
7       any  party’s  claim  or  defense  and  proportional  to  the  needs  of  the  case, 
        considering the importance of the issues at stake in the action, the amount in 
8                                                                            
        controversy, the parties’ relative access to relevant information, the parties’ 
9       resources, the importance of the discovery in resolving the issues, and whether 
        the burden or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit.   
10                                                                            
11  Id.                                                                       
12       Evidence must be “relevant to any party’s claim or defense” to fall within the scope 
13  of permissible discovery.  Id.  The 2015 amendment to Rule 26(b) deleted the phrase 
14  “reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence” because it was 
15  often misconstrued to define the scope of discovery and had the potential to “swallow any 
16  other limitation.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) advisory committee’s notes to 2015 amendment; 
17  see also San Diego Unified Port Dist. v. Nat’l Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburg, PA, No. 
18  15CV1401-BEN-MDD,   2017  WL  3877732,  at  *1  (S.D.  Cal.  Sept.  5,  2017).    The 
19  amendment  replaced  this  phrase  with  the  statement  that  information  “need  not  be 
20  admissible in evidence to be discoverable.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) advisory committee’s 
21  notes to 2015 amendment.                                                  
22       Information must also be “proportional to the needs of the case” to fall within the 
23  scope  of  permissible  discovery.    Fed.  R.  Civ.  P.  26(b)(1).    When  analyzing  the 
24  proportionality of a party’s discovery requests, a court should consider the importance of 
25  the issues at stake in the action, the amount in controversy, the parties’ relative access to 
26  relevant information, the parties’ resources, the importance of the discovery in resolving 
27  the issues, and whether the burden or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its 
28  likely benefit.  Id.                                                      
1       Pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 34, a party may request the production 
2  of documents from another party within the scope of Rule 26(b).  Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(a).  If 
3  a party fails to produce documents pursuant to Rule 34, the propounding party may bring 
4  a motion to compel.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(a).  “The party seeking to compel discovery 
5  has the burden of establishing that its request satisfies the relevancy requirements of Rule 
6  26(b)(1).”  Alves v. Riverside Cnty., 339 F.R.D. 556, 559 (C.D. Cal. 2021) (quoting Bryant 
7  v. Ochoa, No. 07-CV-00200-JM-PCL, 2009 WL 1390794, at *1 (S.D. Cal. May 14, 2009)).  
8  “District courts have broad discretion in determining relevancy for discovery purposes.”  
9  Surfvivor Media, Inc. v. Survivor Prods., 406 F.3d 625, 635 (9th Cir. 2005) (citing Hallett 
10  v. Morgan, 296 F.3d 732, 751 (9th Cir. 2002)).  “Once the propounding party establishes 
11  that the request seeks relevant information, ‘[t]he party who resists discovery has the 
12  burden  to  show  discovery  should  not  be  allowed,  and  has  the  burden  of  clarifying, 
13  explaining, and supporting its objections.’”  Goro v. Flowers Foods, Inc., 334 F.R.D. 275, 
14  283 (S.D. Cal. 2018) (quoting Superior Commc’ns v. Earhugger, Inc., 257 F.R.D. 215, 217 
15  (C.D. Cal. 2009)); see also Blankenship v. Hearst Corp., 519 F.2d 418, 429 (9th Cir. 1975) 
16  (noting those opposing discovery are “required to carry a heavy burden of showing why 
17  discovery [should be] denied”).                                           
18  III.   DISCUSSION                                                         
19       Andrews argues that the requested documents are both relevant and proportional 
20  (ECF No. 37 at 5–6), while Plaintiff contends the request is overbroad based on the scope 
21  of Andrews’ counterclaims, unduly burdensome, and irrelevant (ECF No. 46 at 4–6).3 
22                                                                            
23                                                                            
   3    The  Court  declines  to  address  any  objections  raised  in  Plaintiff’s  discovery 
24                                                                            
   responses that it did not reassert within its opposition brief to the instant Motion.  See Hall 
25  v. Marriott Int’l, Inc., No. 19-cv-01715-JLS-AHG, 2021 WL 1906464, at *9 (S.D. Cal. 
   May 12, 2021) (quoting SolarCity Corp. v. Doria, No. 16-cv-3085-JAH-RBB, 2018 WL 
26                                                                            
   467898, at *3 (S.D. Cal. Jan. 18, 2018)) (“When ruling on a motion to compel, courts in 
27  this district ‘generally consider[ ] only those objections that have been timely asserted in 
   the initial response to the discovery request and that are subsequently reasserted and relied 
28                                                                            
1       A.   Relevance                                                       
2       As a threshold matter, both parties agree that the FY 2022 SIP governs Andrews’ 
3  incentives for the period relevant to her counterclaims.  (Compare ECF Nos. 37 at 4, 50 at 
4  2–3 with ECF No. 46 at 5–6.)  The parties dispute how the contract should be interpreted—
5  namely whether the provisions should be interpreted with the benefit of extrinsic evidence 
6  of the parties’ prior dealings.  Andrews’ counterclaim and Motion both assert a theory of 
7  contract interpretation based on both the written FY 2022 SIP and the parties’ course of 
8  dealings.  (See Countercl. ¶¶ 8, 14, 30; ECF Nos. 37 at 4, 5; 37-2 ¶ 2; 50 at 2, 4–5.)  In its 
9  opposition, Plaintiff repeatedly cites to the FY 2022 SIP provisions, arguing that the 
10  express contract terms overcome Andrews’ course of dealing such that Andrews’ request 
11  is irrelevant.  (ECF No. 46 at 5–6.)                                      
12       “Under California law, the fundamental goal of contract interpretation is to give 
13  effect to the mutual intent of the parties as it existed at the time of contracting.” U.S. 
14  Cellular Inv. Co. v. GTE Mobilnet, Inc., 281 F.3d 929, 934 (9th Cir. 2002) (citing Cal. Civ. 
15  Code § 1636).  “When a contract is reduced to writing, this intent ‘is to be ascertained from 
16  the writing alone, if possible.’”  Id. (quoting Cal. Civ. Code § 1639).  “Under California 
17  law, ‘[t]he test of admissibility of extrinsic evidence to explain the meaning of a written 
18  instrument is not whether it appears to the court to be plain and unambiguous on its face, 
19  but whether the offered evidence is relevant to prove a meaning to which the language of 
20  the instrument is reasonably susceptible.’”  Miller v. Glenn Miller Prods., Inc., 454 F.3d 
21  975, 989 (9th Circ. 2006) (quoting Pac. Gas & Elec. Co. v. G. W. Thomas Drayage & 
22                                                                            
23                                                                            
24                                                                            
   Inc., No. 12-cv-2646-JAH-JMA, 2013 WL 12073836, at *2, n.1 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 4, 2013) 
25  (deeming all objections raised in response to the discovery requests but not addressed in 
   the discovery motion to be moot or waived, and limiting its review to arguments presented 
26                                                                            
   in the parties’ briefs).  Additionally, the Court cautions Plaintiff against objecting on the 
27  ground that a discovery request “is not reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of 
   admissible evidence.”  (ECF Nos. 37-1 at 14, 15; 46 at 2.)  It is time the phrase be retired 
28                                                                            
1  Rigging Co., 442 P.2d 641, 644 (Cal. 1968)).  “Because California law recognizes that the 
2  words of a written instrument often lack a clear meaning apart from the context in which 
3  the words were written, courts may preliminarily consider any extrinsic evidence offered 
4  by the parties.”  Miller, 454 F.3d at 989–90.  “The parties’ ‘prior course of dealings’ is 
5  relevant in this regard.”  Hicks v. PGA Tour, Inc., 897 F.3d 1109, 1118 (9th Cir. 2018). 
6       Here,  Andrews’  course  of  dealings  theory  is  recognized  under  California  law, 
7  making her request for documentation to support her theory relevant.  Plaintiff’s arguments 
8  go to the substantive issue of contract interpretation—an issue not presently before the 
9  Court—rather than to the relevance of the discovery request based on the claims alleged 
10  and defenses asserted.                                                    
11       Andrews’ counterclaim alleges that she was entitled to an incentive payment of 
12  $27,000 for a specific sale of a product shipped to her territory, under the belief that the 
13  FY 2022 SIP combined with the parties’ “long-term course of dealings . . . require payment 
14  for sales of Consumable or Instruments shipped to [Andrews’] territory.”  (ECF No. 37 at 
15  4.)  In the instant Motion, Andrews argues RFP No. 38 is relevant to show that only she 
16  received incentive payments for shipments to her territory from 2019 through 2022.  (ECF 
17  No. 37 at 4–5.)  Additionally, Andrews theorizes that evidence of no employee receiving 
18  incentive payments for sales shipped to Andrews’ territory would support her theory that 
19  Plaintiff was unjustly enriched by not paying incentive awards as required.  (Id.)  Finally, 
20  Andrews concludes, without explanation or analysis, that the information sought would be 
21  directly relevant to Plaintiff’s third (acting in good faith and with good cause), seventh 
22  (legitimate business reasons and good cause), and eighth affirmative defenses (satisfaction 
23  of duties owed).  (Id. at 5–6.)                                           
24       The  Court  does  not  find  persuasive  Andrews’  conclusion  that  the  information 
25  captured by RFP No. 38 would have any bearing on Plaintiff’s affirmative defenses as 
26  Andrews fails to provide any analysis or explanation to that end.  Nonetheless, the Court 
27  is persuaded that, under Andrews’ theory, evidence demonstrating that only Andrews was 
28  paid for sales shipped to her territory is relevant because it could support that the contract 
1  should be interpreted as Andrews asserts.  Further, the Court finds that evidence that no 
2  employee received the $27,000 incentive award for the specific sale at issue would be 
3  relevant to Andrews’ counterclaim.                                        
4       However, as Plaintiff notes (see ECF No. 46 at 4–5), the scope of RFP No. 38 is far 
5  broader than Andrews’ theories of relevance.  First, her counterclaim does not allege 
6  multiple instances of unpaid incentives.  Rather, Andrews alleges that there was one order 
7  in January 2022, for which she should have received a $27,000 incentive award that 
8  Plaintiff did not pay her.  (Countercl. ¶ 9.)  As such, Andrews’ arguments that responsive 
9  documents  would show  “if  through  house  accounts or otherwise  [Plaintiff] has been 
10  unjustly enriched based on sales of products shipped to Andrews’[s] territory” are not 
11  relevant  to  the  claims  or  defenses  of  this  case  to  the  extent  RFP  No.  38  captures 
12  documentation of sales other than the single sale resulting in the alleged $27,000 incentive 
13  award.  (See ECF No. 37 at 5.)                                            
14       Second, Andrews does not explain how “all documents and communications” are 
15  relevant under the limited theories of relevance she asserts.  Plaintiff argues that Andrews’ 
16  request is “tantamount to a fishing expedition” because “[d]ocuments responsive to this 
17  request will include, but will not be limited to, proprietary Azenta sales information, private 
18  third[-]party financial information, sales incentive plan interpretations, and any and all 
19  related communications involving thousands of other sales—all irrelevant and superfluous 
20  to the sale which comprises the sole subject of Andrews’[s] pleading.”  (ECF No. 46 at 5.)  
21  Although  some  of  Plaintiff’s  concerns  could  sufficiently  be  addressed  through  the 
22  protective order and a privilege log, the Court finds Andrews fails to explain how any 
23  communications would be relevant to the claims alleged and defenses asserted in this 
24  action, or why all documents are necessary based on the narrow theories of relevance she 
25  asserts.  As such, the Court finds RFP No. 38 overbroad as written.       
26       Accordingly,  based  on  Andrews’  counterclaims,  Plaintiff’s  defenses,  and  the 
27  theories of relevance Andrews has asserted in the instant Motion, the Court finds RFP 
28  No. 38 relevant only to the extent that it captures documents sufficient to evidence any and 
1  all incentive awards paid to Plaintiff’s employees, excluding Andrews, based on or related 
2  to the shipping of any product during the period from April 30, 2019, to April 15, 2022, to 
3  buyers in Andrews’ territory.                                             
4       B.   Proportionality                                                 
5       Plaintiff argues that Andrews’ request is disproportionate and unduly burdensome 
6  because reviewing and producing “three years’ worth of documents and communications 
7  for the entire organization . . . would in all likelihood exceed the $27,000 unpaid incentive 
8  payment itself.”  (ECF No. 46 at 5.)  In response, Andrews only argues that because the 
9  documents would be “highly relevant,” the cost of their production is proportional to the 
10  needs of the case.  (ECF No. 50 at 6.)                                    
11       “The  parties  and  the  court  have  a  collective  responsibility  to  consider  the 
12  proportionality of all discovery and consider it in resolving discovery disputes.”  Fed. R. 
13  Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 2015 amendment; see also Scherer v. FCA US, 
14  LLC, 538 F. Supp. 3d 1002, 1006 (S.D. Cal. 2021) (“The inquiry to be conducted under 
15  the proportionality requirement . . . requires input from both sides.”).  Although “[the] party 
16  claiming undue burden or expense ordinarily has far better information—perhaps the only 
17  information—with  respect  to  that  part  of  the  determination,”  the  propounding  party 
18  “should be able to explain the ways in which the underlying information bears on the issues 
19  as that party understands them.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 2015 
20  amendment;  see  also  Lopez  v.  United  States,  No.  15-CV-180-JAH-WVG,  2017  WL 
21  1062581, at *5 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 21, 2017) (“Although there are conflicting views on which 
22  party has the burden of proving proportionality, this Court believes the better approach is 
23  that  both  parties  share  the  responsibility  of  explaining  their  positions  regarding  the 
24  proportionality factors.”) (internal citation omitted).  It is “[t]he court’s responsibility, 
25  using all the information provided by the parties, [] to consider these and all the other 
26  factors in reaching a case-specific determination of the appropriate scope of discovery.”  In 
27  re Bard IVC Filters Prod. Liab. Litig., 317 F.R.D. 562, 565 (D. Ariz. 2016) (quoting Fed. 
28  R. Civ. P. 26 advisory committee’s note to 2015 amendment).               
l         As revised, the Court finds RFP No. 38 to be proportional.  Because the Court has

6 || year, (see ECF No. 46 at 3-4, 6), the Court finds that production of ten additional quarters

1  II.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                      
2       The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure authorize parties to obtain discovery of any 
3  nonprivileged  information  discoverable  under  Rule  26  if  it  is  (1)  relevant,  and  (2) 
4  proportional to the needs of the case.  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1).  Rule 26(b)(1), as amended 
5  in 2015, provides that parties—                                           
6                                                                            
        may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to 
7       any  party’s  claim  or  defense  and  proportional  to  the  needs  of  the  case, 
        considering the importance of the issues at stake in the action, the amount in 
8                                                                            
        controversy, the parties’ relative access to relevant information, the parties’ 
9       resources, the importance of the discovery in resolving the issues, and whether 
        the burden or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit.   
10                                                                            
11  Id.                                                                       
12       Evidence must be “relevant to any party’s claim or defense” to fall within the scope 
13  of permissible discovery.  Id.  The 2015 amendment to Rule 26(b) deleted the phrase 
14  “reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence” because it was 
15  often misconstrued to define the scope of discovery and had the potential to “swallow any 
16  other limitation.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) advisory committee’s notes to 2015 amendment; 
17  see also San Diego Unified Port Dist. v. Nat’l Union Fire Ins. Co. of Pittsburg, PA, No. 
18  15CV1401-BEN-MDD,
2017 WL 3877732
,  at  *1  (S.D.  Cal.  Sept.  5,  2017).    The 
19  amendment  replaced  this  phrase  with  the  statement  that  information  “need  not  be 
20  admissible in evidence to be discoverable.”  Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1) advisory committee’s 
21  notes to 2015 amendment.                                                  
22       Information must also be “proportional to the needs of the case” to fall within the 
23  scope  of  permissible  discovery.    Fed.  R.  Civ.  P.  26(b)(1).    When  analyzing  the 
24  proportionality of a party’s discovery requests, a court should consider the importance of 
25  the issues at stake in the action, the amount in controversy, the parties’ relative access to 
26  relevant information, the parties’ resources, the importance of the discovery in resolving 
27  the issues, and whether the burden or expense of the proposed discovery outweighs its 
28  likely benefit.
Id.

2  of documents from another party within the scope of Rule 26(b).  Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(a).  If 
3  a party fails to produce documents pursuant to Rule 34, the propounding party may bring 
4  a motion to compel.  See Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(a).  “The party seeking to compel discovery 
5  has the burden of establishing that its request satisfies the relevancy requirements of Rule

 (9th Cir. 2005) (citing Hallett
